purpose: Show how a short-lived mRNA payload is delivered, translated, sensed and converted into immune memory while distinguishing observed human responses from less certain mechanistic detail.
title: How a temporary RNA recipe builds immune memory
subtitle: Delivery and immune memory are well observed; detailed sensing pathways remain less certain
story: A lipid nanoparticle protects modified mRNA and enables cell entry.
A ribosome reads the single-stranded mRNA in the cytoplasm and briefly produces antigen.
Antigen display and innate signalling coordinate immune activity in a draining lymph node.
The response produces antibodies, memory B cells, and helper and killer T cells.
observed: The RNA remains in the cytoplasm, expression is temporary, and the RNA is degraded.
Human lymph-node responses have been observed for 12 weeks to 6 months.
inferred: Detailed innate-sensing pathways and lipid-nanoparticle adjuvanticity are supported mainly by mouse evidence; mark the signalling stage with a thin dashed boundary and the qualifier mainly mouse evidence.
layout_notes: Use one continuous left-to-right pathway on a white canvas, not four dashboard cards.
Give each stage one refined biological illustration and a lower-case bold panel letter a, b, c or d.
Keep all labels outside busy biological structures with short black leaders.
Place a compact three-line key along the bottom without a box, icon, banner or decorative background.
constraints: Depict mRNA as one flexible single strand, never as a DNA double helix or ladder.
Do not show mRNA entering the nucleus or altering DNA.
Use restrained 2D biological illustration with consistent line weight and no glossy rendering.
The signalling qualifier must be visually distinct without making the stage look unimportant.
avoid: cell nuclei near the mRNA pathway
virus particles presented as vaccine contents
